items.title: Formally verifying agent-written full-stack web apps with PDD Kit
items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for.  PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line.  The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation.  This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an…

items.content: The AI Engineer YouTube channel just crossed one million subscribers . Thank you to everyone who’s watched a talk, sent one to a teammate, or put something they learned into production. For this special, we wanted to sit down with someone who has to answer a question a lot of us are asking at work: what should a software engineer actually learn now? Mihail Eric has two places to test his answer. He teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, where his colleagues use coding agents to ship software and investigate outages. I asked him to take us through the syllabus, then tell us which parts survived contact with his own engineering team. This is also meant as a preview for all of you joining us in San Francisco for AIE Code next week, as required knowledge for all the conversations with the speakers, sponsors and attendees you’re about to have. If you can see this as a LS subscriber and haven’t got a ticket yet, you can use this code for 30% off (no refunds, sorry) Last year’s homework takes one prompt The first run of CS146S had nine assignments and a capstone. In one exercise, students ran an AI code reviewer on a repo and evaluated its feedback. By the next run, Mihail figured students could one-shot a lot of those exercises. When he asked a room of Stanford sophomores and juniors how they coded, everyone he surveyed was already using an agent. So this time, part of the homework is contributing to an open-source project. The person who maintains the repo reviews the student’s patch. I like what that does to the assignment. You can ask an agent to implement a feature in an afternoon. You still have to find out whether the maintainer wants it, why the code behaves the way it does, and what else your patch might break. That conversation is also how a junior engineer gets to learn from a senior one. There’s an exercise in the episode you can borrow for your next PR. items.title: [One Million AI Engineer Special] How Stanford Teaches AI-Native Engineering — Mihail Eric, Monaco
items.content: What do you assign when a coding agent can finish last year’s homework in one prompt? In the second run of Stanford’s CS146S, Mihail Eric brought open-source maintainers into the course. Students have to learn an unfamiliar repo, propose a change, and explain the patch to the person who might merge it. We invited Mihail, who teaches The Modern Software Developer at Stanford and leads AI at Monaco, to celebrate one million subscribers on the AI Engineer YouTube channel. He opens up the course syllabus and shows us which lessons survived contact with his own engineering team. Monaco built its agent workspaces, bought its code review tools, and gave an on-call agent access to Datadog and GitHub. We ask how he decides which tools his team needs to own. items.title: [AINews] LLMs can read & write neural network weights: "Weight Space Programming" cuts Autoresearch out of the RSI loop
items.content: Amid a deepening bear market for AI/tech (worthy of dark humor ) with Anthropic bonds receiving a “junk” rating and OpenAI fundraise headlines , we continue to see very surprising capability finds in the community, such as today. The best way to put today’s blockbuster paper in context is to recall Karpathy’s autoresearch from a mere 8 months ago , which presaged a summer of recursive self improvement fears : Abstractly, the demonstration is that you can take a sufficiently smart model and through running a series of experiments across a compute cluster, train a model autonomously without human expertise or intervention. However, this is usually done by an involved process of writing PyTorch/Jax code and running compute and watching loss curves and reading evals and optimizing kernels and data and…. Well, last month’s guest Alex Zhang comes back to coauthor a MONSTER discovery: what if you just ask a smart model to directly read and edit the weights of a dumber model? View post on X ↗ In ML this is the equivalent of not looking at source code, just directly seeing the 1’s and 0’s of ( very small ) compiled executables, and being able to 1) tell what they do , 2) oneshot-fix bugs given failed traces or, with 50 steps, improve in a general direction ( possible overstatement here ), 3) writing entire network weights from scratch in one shot , beating some independently trained models. If you believe that LLMs can truly fit and simulate everything given enough parameters (and in fact, LLMs are increasingly better calculators as you grow in size), then something like this was in theory bound to happen, but it is surprising nevertheless to have the ability suddenly emerge, as an independent reproduction seems to already have found: View post on X ↗ Of course the exact thing we are really modeling is some variant of mechanistic interpretability (which could be done by hand ), and right now unlikely to scale to more advanced tasks than simple games and RL policies, but the…

items.title: Building AI for Lawyers - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: In this episode, we chat with Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora, following the announcement of their $550M Series E at an $8.8B valuation a couple weeks ago. We talk about what it takes to build AI agents for lawyers and what other people building agents can learn from that work. Legora started in a Stockholm basement with a simple product: ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Jacob had already been through YC with his own startup when he helped Max Junestrand with the application for Leya (now Legora). He later joined as head of engineering and is now CTO. Today the agent drafts and edits Word documents, reviews thousands of contracts at once, and coordinates work between lawyers, their clients, and other agents. The company passed $100 million in ARR in April, less than 18 months after launch, and now has more than 1,800 customers. It raised $550 million in March at a $5.55 billion valuation, then another $550 million in October at an $8.8 billion valuation. Its latest acquisition, Wexler, was its fifth just this year. We asked Jacob how you evaluate agents when you can't see your customers' data, which tasks still need better models, how legal engineers and forward deployed engineers split the work, and why the billable hour as a business model is being upended. Watch the full conversation on YouTube → Open video on YouTube ↗ What changed for the billable hour? When Jacob first read Leya's YC application, he had one piece of feedback: people had tried building legal tech a million times, and it never worked. If lawyers bill by the hour, getting faster means earning less. Why would they buy a tool that does that? What changed, he says, is the pressure on firms. In the US, routine work like small reviews is already shifting to flat project fees. Some firms do it for free to hold on to the client. The money moves to M&A, litigation, and time spent with clients. We asked whether that means firms will stop needing paralegals and junior lawyers. Jacob says that's not…

items.title: Building Legal Agents When You Can't See the Data - Jacob Lauritzen, CTO of Legora
items.content: Legora can’t read a single trace of what its agent does for a lawyer. The data belongs to the law firm’s clients. How do you build and test an agent when you can’t see its work? Jacob Lauritzen is the CTO of Legora, one of the fastest-growing companies in legal tech history. The team started in a Stockholm basement with ChatGPT, Swedish law, and a search tool. Today, a lawyer can use Legora to draft and edit Word documents, review 10,000 contracts in a single table, or run due diligence. The agent also coordinates work between lawyers, clients, and other agents. When Legora made its own acquisitions, the team used it for diligence. What we talked about • Why Legora resisted adding a model picker for years, and why it finally added one • Jacob’s estimate that models already do about 60% of legal work well, and why the rest takes a smarter model • How three engineers and three lawyers build test environments modeled on customers’ work, much like the “worlds” used in reinforcement learning • A citation problem where the model got it right 70% of the time, then 99% after one release. Legora didn’t have to change anything. • Why Legora runs everything on Azure and why it doesn’t use ElevenLabs • Tabular Review, the million-cell spreadsheet the industry copied down to the name • How intake works, how agents create lists, and how a list can start another agent • What legal engineers and forward-deployed engineers each do, and who gets to write code • The 300 Spartans slide Jacob used to argue that 20 engineers would be enough forever. Now there are 100, and he still feels short-handed. • Why Jacob finds Fable and Opus too chatty for drafting and likes Astra’s concise writing • Why drafting a long contract is a search problem • Whether model labs will cut off legal tools the way they cut off coding tools • What happens to law firm partnerships, the billable hour, and jobs for junior lawyers Legora is hiring engineers in New York, Stockholm, and London. items.title: Agents Prompt People: Using Agents for Long-Horizon Financial Work
items.content: At AI Engineer New York this month, we sat down with Aman Singh , the lead AI Engineer at Arca , an “AI-native” company providing wealth management services. We discovered that while agents do most of the background work in the firm, there are guardrails in place to ensure that human advisors are making the final decisions. The goal is for AI to guide the process; or as Singh nicely put it, “agents prompt people more than people prompt agents.” Arca recently raised $48.5 Million in a round led by General Catalyst, with participation from Index Ventures and Venrock. One of the features of using AI in financial services, explained Singh, is that it’s typically long-horizon work — although not long-running. In his AIE presentation, Singh noted that agent tasks at Arca can take up to ten days. “It's very stop-start, there's many actors in between, many decision points, many handoffs,” he said. For this reason, Arca has developed an internal memory system . “So we have this persistence for every client ,” Singh said in our podcast discussion. “What has happened so far? What are we tracking for next? What needs to happen immediately in the next couple of days [and] what are we tracking for the long term? Which individual is responsible for which action? All of this is being tracked by our memory systems that our agents contribute to.” Arca uses models from frontier labs like Anthropic and OpenAI, with Claude its primary model provider. The company has built its own harness , which automatically selects the best model to use for a particular task, based on the company’s internal benchmarks. Owning the harness, rather than using a managed agent harness, also means that Arca has the flexibility to change model providers if it needs to. Safety is obviously key for financial services. Singh noted that although agents do much of the work, an agent’s role is limited to analysis and proposing solutions. Trading and any other money movement is handled by a human advisor. “All of…
